source.title: Impact of classification difficulty on the weight matrices spectra in Deep Learning and application to early-stopping

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies batch size and reports held-out accuracy after a fixed 248-epoch training budget on image classifiers, which bears on V5. It does not measure the generalization gap directly or test the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports spectrum results across SNR, layers, classes, and batch sizes, but these do not measure a claim version's named generalization behavior. Table 8's final-epoch held-out accuracies are retained for V5. Early-stopping comparisons and synthetic-data accuracy results do not compare batch sizes and are not rows for V5.
record.test_reason: Table 8 compares held-out accuracy across batch sizes at a fixed 248-epoch budget, directly testing V5 with momentum SGD on MNIST and CIFAR10. The study is not an original source for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify classification difficulty as a driver of heavy-tailed weight spectra and propose a spectral early-stopping criterion that often saves training with comparable test accuracy and can detect overfitting or instability. They do not establish that heavy tails uniformly imply better generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines weight-matrix spectra and a spectral early-stopping rule. For the V5-relevant results, it compares batch sizes with training runs at 248 epochs; it does not test the original large-batch generalization-gap methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size and dataset are reported to change final test accuracy and spectrum type.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower signal-to-noise ratio, more classes, and complex image features make heavy-tailed weight spectra more likely.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Classification difficulty affects the spectral distribution of trained weight matrices.

fits_no_version.finding: A criterion based on departure from the Marchenko–Pastur spectrum selects early stopping times that can save training and sometimes avoid overfitting or collapse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-spectrum statistics can guide early stopping without held-out data.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are stated for the batch-size results. The reported accuracies do not directly quantify the training-to-test gap. For MiniAlexNet+CIFAR10 at batch sizes 16 and 32, the final-epoch table reports 10% (explode), so these are not directly comparable to the other final accuracies.
record.rows_left_out: Early-stopping results in Tables 7, 8, 9, and 10 are omitted because they compare the spectral stopping rule with the final epoch rather than compare batch sizes as V5 specifies. Synthetic data, spectral transitions, and spectra-by-batch-size results are also omitted because they do not report V5's held-out accuracy comparison across batch sizes.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Test-error changes when widening beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning budgets, switching optimizers, and decoupled weight decay.
Language models, longer-training remedies, learning-rate scaling and warmup, normalization or regularization changes, and the batch-size threshold beyond the tested range of 16–256.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All judgments use the supplied text. Table 10 repeats the final accuracies and confirms R12 should be 99.41%. No uncertainty estimates accompany these comparisons. A training-to-test gap is unnecessary for V5's held-out-performance comparison. Equality at batches 16 and 32 does not challenge a claim whose adverse-effect threshold is workload dependent. The small-batch collapse qualifies the comparison rather than refuting the larger-batch penalty among stable runs.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep tied to test error after reaching zero training error.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.
No language models or direct measurement of the training-to-test generalization gap; the reported real-data results compare final held-out accuracy at 248 epochs across batch sizes.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measure or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
